title: Bali keeps his word
hookLine: a teacher warns the king that the small boy is Vishnu, and the king keeps his promise anyway
carry: truth kept, and the self offered to God
tomorrow: where does a god send the king who gave him everything?

cards: The water pot is already tilted. In the old way of giving a gift, the giver pours water to seal the promise, and Bali is about to pour. Then his teacher, Shukra, pulls him aside.
Shukra sees what the king doesn't: that small boy is Vishnu. Give him three steps and he will take everything you have. Take your word back, he says.
Here, even a teacher thinks a lie would be wiser. Today, what a good king does with a promise that's about to cost him the world.

teach.b: The Bhagavata Purana gives Shukra a strong case.
He tells Bali that this boy is Vishnu in disguise, and that the gift will strip him of everything. He even argues that in some moments, an untrue word is allowed. Bali hears him out, and refuses.
In paraphrase: I am Prahlada's grandson. I have said I will give. I will not take it back.
And the text puts a striking line in his mouth: the earth can carry any weight except the weight of a liar. So Bali pours the water. Shukra, angry, curses him to lose his fortune.
Then the small boy begins to grow, past the trees, past the sky, until he holds the worlds inside his body. With one step he covers the earth. With the second, the heavens.
There's nowhere left for the third. Bali's soldiers rush at the giant, and Bali stops them. He is bound with ropes.

teach.h: THE THIRD STEP ON HIS HEAD
teach.b: And Vamana asks: where does my third step go? Bali answers: put it on my head. Hindu teachers hear two teachings here.
The first is satya, truth, one of the oldest pillars of dharma: for Bali, a broken word weighs more than three lost worlds. The second is bhakti at its deepest.
In the Bhagavata, Prahlada lists nine ways of loving God, from hearing God's name to offering your whole self.
Many Vaishnava teachers name Bali as the great example of that last one, atma-nivedana, the self offered. He bowed his head, and let God's foot rest on it.

how: At Onam, Keralites retell how Mahabali kept his word to Vamana and offered his head for the third step, and the Bhagavata Purana's account of it is read and recited in the season.

games.q: what does “kerala's onam and ayyappa” mean?
o: a festival for a king who kept his word at any cost
a festival for a king who broke his word to save his throne
a festival for the teacher who warned the king in time

games.q: the three steps — tap the pairs.
p: warned the king: take your word back

s: Shukra urged Bali to keep his promise
his teacher urged him to take it back, and argued that an untrue word is sometimes allowed.
Vaishnava teachers hold up Bali as the example of offering your whole self to God
atma-nivedana, the self offered, is the last of the nine ways of devotion Prahlada lists, and Bali's bowed head is its classic picture.
in the text, the earth cannot bear the weight of a liar
the Bhagavata gives Bali that line as his reason for keeping his word.

games.q: you're Bali. your teacher says the boy is Vishnu and will take everything. the water pot is in your hands. what do you do?
o: take your word back, as your teacher says.
pour the water and keep your promise.
offer the boy a smaller gift instead.
games.why: Bali keeps his word: satya, truth, outweighs three worlds. he loses everything in two steps, and offers his own head for the third.

practice: Hold one promise you've made that's still open, to a friend, a parent, God, yourself, the way Bali held the water pot. Ask quietly what keeping it would cost, and what breaking it would cost.
Then breathe out and let your head bow a little, the way Bali bowed his. If you pray, offer the day with that bow.

wordCard.voice: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, Bali's choice: warned that the boy was Vishnu, he kept his word, and offered his own head for the third step. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Trivikrama, 'of the three strides', a name of Vishnu for the giant Vamana becomes.

carryVoice: Your line: truth kept, and the self offered to God. Bali lost three worlds and kept both. Go gently.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.19.30–8.20.15 (Shukra's warning; Bali's reply; the earth and the weight of a liar)
Bhagavata Purana 8.20.16–8.22.3 (the gift sealed with water; Vamana grows; two steps; Bali bound; the third step on his head)
